title: Annealed Lévy Diffusion via Gaussian Surrogate Reverse Dynamics

paper.title: Annealed Lévy Diffusion via Gaussian Surrogate Reverse Dynamics
paper.abstract:
Abstract Gaussian diffusion models ( Ho et al., 2020 ) offer a practical framework for generative modeling.
Denoising Lévy Probabilistic Models (DLPM) ( Shariatian et al., 2025 ) introduce heavy-tailed perturbations with a fixed tail index throughout denoising.
We introduce Annealed Lévy Diffusion (ALD) .
ALD varies the stability index α ⁡ ( t ) \alpha(t) to combine heavy-tailed exploration with Gaussian refinement.
Our marginal-first formulation represents stable noise as a scalar Gaussian scale mixture.
This formulation enables standard Gaussian noise-prediction training with one additional scale input.
We study two sampling processes.
ALD-renoise estimates the clean sample and injects fresh marginal noise.
ALD-posterior preserves dependence between successive states through an accumulated conditional variance and a Gaussian bridge update.
Both samplers reuse the same trained predictor with different scalar inputs.
We evaluate ALD on four 2D benchmarks and an imbalanced nine-mode mixture.
We also examine training efficiency and the effects of prediction perturbations on clipped Holtsmark data.
Additional experiments evaluate MNIST and CelebA64 generation and CIFAR-10LT augmentation.
ALD preserves local geometry on the evaluated light-tailed and manifold-structured targets.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion models ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Song and Ermon, 2020 ; Ho et al., 2020 ) have established themselves as the dominant paradigm for high-fidelity generative modeling, with applications spanning image synthesis ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ) and scientific problems ( Pandey et al., 2025 ; Watson et al., 2023 ; Zeni et al., 2025 ) . Their core mechanism is to corrupt data 𝐱 0 ∼ p data \mathbf{x}_{0}\sim p_{\mathrm{data}} via a fixed stochastic process and learn to reverse it: the forward process produces 𝐱 t = m t ​ 𝐱 0 + σ t ​ 𝐧 \mathbf{x}_{t}=m_{t}\mathbf{x}_{0}+\sigma_{t}\mathbf{n} with 𝐧 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝐈 ) \mathbf{n}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}) , and generation proceeds via the estimated reverse kernel p θ ​ ( 𝐱 t − 1 ∣ 𝐱 t ) p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t-1}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}) . The common choice of Gaussian noise is motivated by analytical tractability: it admits closed-form forward kernels, a stable ϵ \epsilon -prediction objective, and a reverse-time SDE representation under suitable regularity conditions via Anderson’s time-reversal formula ( Anderson, 1982 ) . However, for target distributions with polynomial tails, the Gaussian terminal prior and light-tailed perturbation kernels provide exponentially weaker relative coverage of extreme regions than the data law. With finite samples and training budgets, the network therefore struggles to estimate the score accurately in the tail regions due to the scarcity of training samples there. This score estimation difficulty is consequential for a broad and scientifically important class of problems. The Holtsmark distribution describes Coulomb force statistics from random point charges and is a 3 / 2 3/2 -stable distribution ( α = 3 / 2 \alpha=3/2 , with PDF decaying as | x | − 5 / 2 |x|^{-5/2} ) ( Holtsmark, 1919 ; Samorodnitsky and Taqqu, 1994 ; Nolan, 2020 ) ; financial return distributions can exhibit power-law tails, motivating heavy-tailed alternatives to Gaussian models ( Gopikrishnan et al., 1999 ; Nolan, 2020 ; Larralde and Mota Navarro, 2025 ) ; heavy-tailed statistics also arise in fluid dynamics and related transport phenomena, as illustrated by studies of anomalous transport and turbulence spreading ( Solomon et al., 1993 ; Buonocore et al., 2020 ; Milovanov et al., 2025 ) . For such distributions, Gaussian diffusion can suffer from tail blindness : the terminal prior is light-tailed and the training distribution gives sparse effective coverage to rare extremes, so learned scores in tail regions are poorly constrained and may collapse toward bulk-dominated behavior. This bias is not merely a representational limitation: increasing capacity alone does not repair the sparse far-tail coverage induced by Gaussian corruption ( Song and Ermon, 2019 ; Yu and Yu, 2026 ) ; see also Experiment 5.3 . The natural remedy is to replace Gaussian noise with α \alpha -stable Lévy noise ( Applebaum, 2009 ) , whose tail probability decays polynomially as Pr ⁡ ( | z | > x ) ∼ C α ​ x − α \Pr(|z|>x)\sim C_{\alpha}x^{-\alpha} for α ∈ ( 0 , 2 ) \alpha\in(0,2) ; at the boundary α = 2 \alpha=2 the distribution reduces to the Gaussian, whose tails decay exponentially and the polynomial formula no longer applies. This provides a parametric family that can be matched to infinite-variance polynomial-tail targets with tail exponent in ( 0 , 2 ) (0,2) by choosing α \alpha appropriately. However, prior attempts encounter one of two fundamental obstructions. Continuous Lévy–Itô SDE approaches such as LIM ( Yoon et al., 2023 ) require a reverse-time formulation adapted to jump-driven dynamics. Although Lévy processes are semimartingales and admit Itô calculus, the Brownian reverse-SDE formula based on the ordinary score ∇ 𝐱 ​ log ​ p t ​ ( 𝐱 ) \nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\log p_{t}(\mathbf{x}) cannot be applied directly. For isotropic α \alpha -stable noise with α < 2 \alpha<2 , the generator is nonlocal and involves the fractional Laplacian − ( − Δ ) α / 2 -(-\Delta)^{\alpha/2} . LIM derives the corresponding reverse-time formulation using a nonlocal fractional score and learns it through fractional denoising score matching, introducing additional analytical complexity relative to Gaussian diffusion. Discrete Markov chain models such as DLPM ( Shariatian et al., 2025 ) avoid this fractional-score formulation by representing stable noise as a scalar Gaussian scale mixture and deriving approximate reverse updates through conditional Gaussian posterior calculations. Their explicit stable marginal laws rely on convolution closure among independent α \alpha -stable increments with a common stability index. DLPM therefore keeps α \alpha fixed throughout the chain; varying the index would generally take the accumulated noise outside the stable family used in its derivation. Although the noise amplitude can decrease during denoising, this fixed-index construction does not support independently annealing the tail index toward the Gaussian boundary α = 2 \alpha=2 during final refinement. This leaves no tail-index schedule for assigning different tail behavior to exploration and geometry refinement. Recent theoretical and empirical work also identifies a trade-off between improved initialization and the statistical difficulty of reverse estimation under heavy-tailed noising ( Cherkaoui et al., 2026 ) . These paradigms expose complementary modeling constraints: jump-driven formulations require nonlocal reverse operators, while standard fixed-index stable chains do not provide a tail-index schedule. This motivates constructions that keep conditional Gaussian calculations tractable without requiring stable closure across time. We introduce Annealed Lévy Diffusion (ALD) to address the fixed-index restriction through a marginal-first construction that specifies α ⁡ ( t ) \alpha(t) -stable perturbation kernels directly at each time. By retaining a scalar Gaussian scale-mixture representation, ALD allows α ⁡ ( t ) \alpha(t) to vary while preserving tractable conditional Gaussian calculations and standard Gaussian noise-prediction training with one additional scale input. The resulting schedule combines heavy-tailed exploration with Gaussian refinement. We adopt a marginal-first formulation related to diffusion models with location-scale noise ( Jolicoeur-Martineau et al., 2023 ) . Instead of deriving the forward process from discrete convolution or a Lévy SDE, we define the perturbed state directly via the sub-Gaussian representation of an α ⁡ ( t ) \alpha(t) -stable vector: 𝐱 t = m t ​ 𝐱 0 + σ t ​ S t ​ 𝐧 , S t ∼ 𝒜 α ⁡ ( t ) / 2 , 𝐧 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝐈 ) , \mathbf{x}_{t}=m_{t}\mathbf{x}_{0}+\sigma_{t}\sqrt{S_{t}}\,\mathbf{n},\quad S_{t}\sim\mathcal{A}_{\alpha(t)/2},\quad\mathbf{n}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}), where 𝒜 α ⁡ ( t ) / 2 \mathcal{A}_{\alpha(t)/2} is a positive ( α ⁡ ( t ) / 2 ) (\alpha(t)/2) -stable variance multiplier ( Samorodnitsky and Taqqu, 1994 , Sec. 2.5, Prop. 2.5.2) . Because 𝐱 t \mathbf{x}_{t} is not derived from convolution of historical increments, α ⁡ ( t ) \alpha(t) can be any prescribed function of t t , enabling a two-phase annealing schedule that transitions from heavy-tailed exploration ( t ≥ τ t\geq\tau ) to pure Gaussian refinement ( t < τ t<\tau , S t ≡ 1 S_{t}\equiv 1 ). The reverse process is a discrete ancestral sampler: conditioned on S t S_{t} , the forward likelihood and denoising score target are Gaussian, so training reduces to standard Gaussian score matching with a single additional scalar input log ⁡ S t \log S_{t} . The practical samplers reconstruct a clean-data estimate with a Gaussian noise predictor. We study direct marginal re-noising (ALD-renoise) and a variance-controlled adjacent transition (ALD-posterior) that retains the current-state contribution and tracks the accumulated conditional noise variance.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: Our central contribution is a marginal-first construction that uses time-dependent α ⁡ ( t ) \alpha(t) -stable perturbation kernels and conditional Gaussian noise prediction. This construction permits a two-phase schedule from heavy-tailed exploration to Gaussian refinement and can reuse standard diffusion backbones with a scalar scale-conditioning input. We provide two practical reverse updates, ALD-renoise and ALD-posterior, which share a trained predictor but differ in adjacent-state coupling. Through experiments on synthetic and image datasets, we analyze tail recovery, geometric fidelity, and sensitivity to prediction errors, and evaluate the effectiveness of ALD for downstream data augmentation.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Score-based generative models Song and Ermon (2020) ; Ho et al. (2020) learn to reverse diffusion via score estimation; the score SDE framework Song et al. (2021a) unifies discrete and continuous approaches, identifying the probability flow ODE as a deterministic counterpart to the reverse SDE. Flow Matching Lipman et al. (2023) ; Liu et al. (2023) regresses directly on conditional velocity fields, while Stochastic Interpolants Albergo et al. (2025) ; Ma et al. (2024) subsume both perspectives by deriving smooth marginal velocity fields from algebraic interpolation. Among heavy-tailed generative models, DLPM Shariatian et al. (2025) replaces Gaussian noise with fixed- α \alpha stable noise in a discrete Markov chain via convolution closure; LIM Yoon et al. (2023) embeds α \alpha -stable Lévy processes into a continuous SDE and derives a reverse process via fractional denoising score matching; t-EDM and t-Flow Pandey et al. (2025) use Student-t distributions with a fixed Student-t tail parameter under the EDM framework. DLPM and LIM use a fixed stable index, while t-EDM and t-Flow use a fixed Student-t tail parameter. ALD prescribes a time-dependent stable index through a conditional Gaussian scale-mixture formulation. Cold Diffusion Bansal et al. (2023) studies more general image degradations, including deterministic transforms such as blur and masking, rather than requiring stable-noise perturbations. The sub-Gaussian representation 𝐳 = d S ​ 𝐧 \mathbf{z}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\sqrt{S}\,\mathbf{n} is classical Samorodnitsky and Taqqu (1994) ; Feller (1971) and has been exploited in robust statistics and neural network weight analysis Hodgkinson and Mahoney (2021) ; we use it as the structural foundation of our marginal-first forward process. ALD’s two-phase annealing draws philosophical inspiration from Annealed Importance Sampling Neal (2001) and parallel tempering Swendsen and Wang (1986) , but performs annealing within a single continuous-time reverse trajectory via the dynamic α ⁡ ( t ) \alpha(t) parameter.

sections.heading: 3.2 Heavy-Tailed Diffusion: DLPM
sections.text: DLPM Shariatian et al. (2025) extends the above by replacing the Gaussian noise 𝐧 \mathbf{n} with α \alpha -stable noise. A non-degenerate random variable X X is α \alpha -stable , with stability index α ∈ ( 0 , 2 ] \alpha\in(0,2] , if, for every integer n ≥ 2 n\geq 2 , independent random variables X 1 , … , X n X_{1},\ldots,X_{n} having the same distribution as X X satisfy X 1 + ⋯ + X n = d n 1 / α ​ X + d n X_{1}+\cdots+X_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}n^{1/\alpha}X+d_{n} for some constant d n ∈ ℝ d_{n}\in\mathbb{R} . For α ∈ ( 0 , 2 ) \alpha\in(0,2) , the distribution is heavy-tailed with polynomial tail Pr ⁡ ( | X | > x ) ∼ C α ​ x − α \Pr(|X|>x)\sim C_{\alpha}x^{-\alpha} , where the stability index α \alpha directly controls the polynomial decay rate. The boundary case α = 2 \alpha=2 is Gaussian, whose tails decay exponentially—it does not satisfy the polynomial formula above. DLPM defines the forward process as a discrete Markov chain with transition 𝐱 ( k ) | 𝐱 ( k − 1 ) , S k ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( γ k ​ 𝐱 ( k − 1 ) , σ k 2 ​ S k ​ 𝐈 ) , S k ∼ 𝒜 α / 2 . \mathbf{x}^{(k)}\mid\mathbf{x}^{(k-1)},S_{k}\sim\mathcal{N}\!\left(\gamma_{k}\mathbf{x}^{(k-1)},\sigma_{k}^{2}S_{k}\mathbf{I}\right),\qquad S_{k}\sim\mathcal{A}_{\alpha/2}. By convolution closure (the sum of two independent α \alpha -stable variables with the same α \alpha is again α \alpha -stable), the marginals admit the closed-form Gaussian scale-mixture representation 𝐱 ( k ) ∣ 𝐱 0 = d m ¯ k 𝐱 0 + σ ¯ k S ¯ k 𝐧 , S ¯ k ∼ 𝒜 α / 2 , 𝐧 ∼ 𝒩 ( 𝟎 , 𝐈 ) , S ¯ k ⟂ 𝐧 . \mathbf{x}^{(k)}\mid\mathbf{x}_{0}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\bar{m}_{k}\mathbf{x}_{0}+\bar{\sigma}_{k}\sqrt{\bar{S}_{k}}\,\mathbf{n},\qquad\bar{S}_{k}\sim\mathcal{A}_{\alpha/2},\qquad\mathbf{n}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}),\qquad\bar{S}_{k}\perp\mathbf{n}. Fixed-index heavy-tailed perturbations can introduce spurious extremes near geometric structures, as illustrated by our evaluated 2D benchmarks (Section 5.2 ). If independent stable increments have different indices, their sum is generally not stable, so the fixed-index marginal representation above does not directly extend to a time-varying index. A different construction is therefore needed to prescribe stable perturbations with a varying index. This modeling constraint motivates our marginal-first formulation.

sections.heading: Schedule for time-varying α ⁡ ( t ) \alpha(t) .
sections.text: Intuitively, we use α ⁡ ( t ) \alpha(t) to establish a two-phase denoising dynamic. In the early exploration phase ( t > τ t>\tau ), heavy-tailed perturbations are intended to facilitate exploration across low-density inter-mode regions. In the subsequent refinement phase ( t ≤ τ t\leq\tau ), the perturbation becomes Gaussian ( S t ≡ 1 S_{t}\equiv 1 ), reducing large noise impulses near the data manifold. To realize this mechanism, we adopt a piecewise linear schedule (Figure 1 ): α ⁡ ( t ) = { 2 − ( 2 − α min ) ​ ( t − τ ) 1 − τ , t ≥ τ , 2 , t < τ , \alpha(t)=\begin{cases}2-\dfrac{(2-\alpha_{\min})(t-\tau)}{1-\tau},&t\geq\tau,\\[6.0pt] 2,&t<\tau,\end{cases} (8) where τ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ) \tau\in[0,1) denotes the phase-transition threshold and α min ∈ ( 1 , 2 ) \alpha_{\min}\in(1,2) bounds the tail heaviness. As demonstrated in Section 5 , this schedule yields clear empirical benefits: • On light-tailed and manifold heavy-tailed benchmarks, ALD matches the performance of DDPM, while the DLPM may exhibit a heavy-tail hallucination (Section 5.2 ). • On globally heavy-tailed distributions, ALD strictly outperforms DDPM while incurring substantially lower training costs (Sections 5.2 , 5.3 ). • Across all evaluated settings, ALD consistently achieves higher sample fidelity than DLPM (Section 5.2 ).

sections.heading: 5 Numerical Experiments
sections.text: We study distributional fidelity on synthetic targets, training efficiency on heavy-tailed data, image generation on MNIST and CelebA64, and downstream data augmentation on CIFAR-10LT. Each experiment states its objective, dataset, protocol, and findings.

sections.heading: Models and metrics.
sections.text: We compare ALD with DDPM Ho et al. (2020) and DLPM Shariatian et al. (2025) . DDPM uses Gaussian corruption, DLPM a fixed stability index, and ALD the schedule α ⁡ ( t ) \alpha(t) with clamped scale S ~ t \tilde{S}_{t} . We report sliced W 2 W_{2} and Gaussian-kernel MMD 2 \mathrm{MMD}^{2} as standard distributional metrics; lower is better. Their estimators, bandwidth rule, sampling parameters, and reporting conventions are given in Appendix A . For CelebA64 image generation, we additionally report Fréchet Inception Distance (FID), Kernel Inception Distance (KID), and feature-space precision, recall, density, and coverage. Lower FID and KID and higher precision, recall, density, and coverage are preferred. The evaluation protocol is specified in Section 5.6 .

sections.text: We use a heavy-tailed cross (HTC), a Swiss Roll manifold, a forty-component Gaussian mixture (MoG40), and a Holtsmark distribution as the four main 2D benchmarks, together with an imbalanced nine-mode Gaussian mixture for mode-mass recovery. For the four main benchmarks, each comparison uses five seeds and matched reference samples. ALD-renoise uses dataset-specific sampling configurations. Sampling configurations are selected on validation streams and frozen before final evaluation. Dataset constructions, architectures, training budgets, clipping bounds, and ALD-posterior selection details are reported in Appendix A . sections.heading: Results and discussion.
sections.text: The 2D results show that ALD achieves competitive generation quality on light-tailed and manifold-structured data, with ALD-posterior providing stronger performance on heavy-tailed data. On the light-tailed MoG40 benchmark and the manifold-structured HTC and Swiss Roll benchmarks, ALD-renoise and ALD-posterior achieve generation quality comparable to DDPM and better than DLPM (Figure 2 ). This behavior is consistent with ALD’s Gaussian refinement phase, which helps recover local geometry after heavy-tailed exploration. On the heavy-tailed Holtsmark benchmark, ALD-posterior performs best among all compared methods (Table 2 ). This result supports combining Lévy exploration with the variance-controlled posterior transition to capture global tail structure.

sections.heading: Training budget and prediction accuracy.
sections.text: ALD-renoise and ALD-posterior share the same noise-prediction training formulation. In the Holtsmark experiments, ALD-renoise performs better at smaller training budgets, whereas ALD-posterior becomes more effective after more training updates. These results suggest that the preferred sampler depends on prediction accuracy. The controlled prediction-output perturbation experiment further supports this tradeoff: ALD-renoise is less sensitive to perturbation added to the network’s predictions, while ALD-posterior achieves better generation quality without this added noise, as observed in the Holtsmark experiment (Appendix A.3 ).

sections.heading: Mathematical interpretation of ALD-posterior.
sections.text: The forward perturbation in Eq. ( 6 ) specifies the distribution at each time but leaves the dependence between times unspecified. Whether the process is Markovian cannot be determined from these marginal distributions alone. ALD-posterior introduces an explicit Markov forward process through Eq. ( 11 ), with accumulated conditional variance V t V_{t} given by Eq. ( 12 ). This construction replaces the original conditional noise variance σ t 2 ​ S t \sigma_{t}^{2}S_{t} by V t V_{t} and generally changes the intermediate marginal distributions. It nevertheless retains the same initial data distribution, since m 0 = 1 m_{0}=1 and V 0 = 0 V_{0}=0 . For this new forward process, Gaussian conditioning gives an exact adjacent posterior when the clean sample 𝐱 0 \mathbf{x}_{0} and the relevant variance variables are known. During generation, 𝐱 0 \mathbf{x}_{0} is replaced by the denoiser 𝐱 ^ 0 P \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{\mathrm{P}} . The resulting Gaussian approximation omits the contribution of clean-data posterior uncertainty to the reverse covariance. ALD-posterior is thus a variance-controlled reverse sampler for an alternative forward process, whose intermediate marginals differ from those used by ALD-renoise.

sections.heading: Conclusion.
sections.text: We proposed Annealed Lévy Diffusion (ALD), which combines heavy-tailed exploration with Gaussian refinement while retaining conditionally Gaussian noise-prediction training. Experiments on synthetic and image benchmarks show competitive generation quality, rare-mode coverage, and training efficiency.

sections.text: We reuse the three ALD checkpoints with H = 256 H=256 and K = 1,000 K=1{,}000 from the Holtsmark efficiency study and perturb every network output as ϵ 𝜽 + σ noise ​ 𝐳 \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}+\sigma_{\mathrm{noise}}\mathbf{z} , where 𝐳 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝐈 2 ) \mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}_{2}) and σ noise ∈ { 0 , 0.05 , 0.1 , 0.25 , 0.5 , 0.75 , 1 } \sigma_{\mathrm{noise}}\in\{0,0.05,0.1,0.25,0.5,0.75,1\} . Each checkpoint is sampled three times, giving nine runs per condition; every run compares 5,000 generated and 5,000 reference samples. All other settings are shared. ALD-renoise makes 74 network calls because the endpoint t = 1 t=1 uses the empirical data mean, whereas ALD-posterior makes 75. Figure 6: Prediction-output perturbation on Holtsmark (mean ± \pm sample standard deviation over nine runs). Lower is better for W 2 W_{2} and MMD 2 \mathrm{MMD}^{2} ; SHS is ranked by distance to one. Both samplers reuse the same ALD checkpoints and differ only in the reverse transition. Without perturbation, ALD-posterior has the lower W 2 W_{2} and MMD 2 \mathrm{MMD}^{2} . Small perturbations leave ALD-renoise nearly unchanged but already increase the posterior W 2 W_{2} ; by σ noise = 0.25 \sigma_{\mathrm{noise}}=0.25 , ALD-renoise has the lower W 2 W_{2} , and the gap widens thereafter. The improvement of ALD-renoise at intermediate noise levels should not be interpreted as monotone robustness: the added prediction noise expands its initially concentrated samples, while its W 2 W_{2} and MMD 2 \mathrm{MMD}^{2} worsen again at σ noise = 1 \sigma_{\mathrm{noise}}=1 . SHS further shows different tail biases—ALD-renoise underproduces directional extremes, whereas ALD-posterior increasingly overproduces them. The experiment therefore supports an accuracy–sensitivity trade-off between the two reverse rules, not uniform superiority of either rule.

sections.heading: A.5 CIFAR-10LT Augmentation Protocol
sections.text: The 100:1 CIFAR-10LT class counts are ( 5000 , 2997 , 1796 , 1077 , 645 , 387 , 232 , 139 , 83 , 50 ) (5000,2997,1796,1077,645,387,232,139,83,50) . All class-conditional generators use the same CIFAR U-Net, batch size 100, learning rate 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} , and 400,000 updates. DDPM and DLPM use 100 diffusion steps, and ALD-posterior uses 100 network evaluations. Each generator produces 50,000 images. A ResNet-18 teacher trained on the 50,000 balanced CIFAR-10 training images assigns hard pseudo-labels without confidence filtering. Each augmentation arm trains a new ResNet-18 from 50,000 real and 50,000 synthetic images. Every batch has 64 real and 64 synthetic images. Training uses 10,000 SGD updates, initial learning rate 0.1, momentum 0.9, weight decay 5 × 10 − 4 5\times 10^{-4} , and cosine learning-rate decay. Evaluation uses the balanced 10,000-image test set. Classwise F 1 is one-vs-rest from the multiclass confusion matrix.

sections.heading: Validation-only ALD sampler selection.
sections.text: Before formal evaluation, we registered nine ALD settings from η ∈ { 0 , 0.5 , 1 } \eta\in\{0,0.5,1\} and time-grid power p ∈ { 1 , 1.5 , 2 } p\in\{1,1.5,2\} . Each setting generated 5,000 images at 1,000 NFE and was evaluated against the independent validation split using all six metrics. We formed the Pareto frontier by minimizing FID and KID and maximizing precision, recall, density, and coverage; from its six nondominated settings, we froze the one with lowest validation FID: ( η , p ) = ( 0.5 , 1.5 ) (\eta,p)=(0.5,1.5) (validation FID 4.5266). The other validation results and tradeoffs are retained in Table 9 . No formal train-reference result was used to change this configuration.

sections.heading: Training and evaluation settings.
sections.text: We use the CelebA64 split with 162,770 training and 19,867 validation images. Following the released LIM preprocessing ( Yoon et al., 2023 ) , the aligned images are cropped to 128 × 128 128\times 128 at top 57 and left 25, resized to 64 × 64 64\times 64 by bilinear interpolation, and normalized to [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] ; random horizontal flipping is used during training. All three models follow the released LIM CelebA U-Net configuration ( Yoon et al., 2023 ) : base width 128, channel multipliers ( 1 , 2 , 2 , 2 , 4 ) (1,2,2,2,4) , two residual blocks per downsampling level, attention at resolution 16 × 16 16\times 16 and in the bottleneck, and dropout 0.1. ALD additionally receives the noise-scale input. Training uses one seed, 600,000 optimizer updates, global batch size 256 (153.6 million image presentations), and an EMA decay of 0.9999. The optimizer is AdamW with zero weight decay, initial learning rate 10 − 4 10^{-4} , linear learning-rate decay without warm-up, and gradient-norm clipping at one. We sample from each final EMA checkpoint with sampling seed 0, generating 50,000 images at 1,000 network evaluations (NFE) per image. The architecture, image count, training budget, EMA, generated count, NFE, and real-image reference protocol are matched, while each method retains its own training objective and reverse sampler.

sections.heading: Evaluation protocol.
sections.text: We extract the same 2,048-dimensional InceptionV3 features for generated and real images using pytorch-fid . FID ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) is the mean and sample standard deviation across five fixed 50,000-image draws from the 162,770-image training pool, compared with the same 50,000 generated images. KID ( Bińkowski et al., 2018 ) uses the unbiased MMD-squared estimator with the degree-three polynomial kernel and is reported as the mean and sample standard deviation across 100 fixed 1,000/1,000 subsets. Precision and recall ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2019 ) use k = 3 k=3 ; density and coverage ( Naeem et al., 2020 ) use k = 5 k=5 , all computed by our implementation on the same fixed 10,000/10,000 real and generated feature subsets. Denoising Lévy Probabilistic Models (DLPM) ( Shariatian et al., 2025 ) introduce heavy-tailed perturbations with a fixed tail index throughout denoising. We introduce Annealed Lévy Diffusion (ALD) . ALD varies the stability index α ⁡ ( t ) \alpha(t) to combine heavy-tailed exploration with Gaussian refinement. Our marginal-first formulation represents stable noise as a scalar Gaussian scale mixture. This formulation enables standard Gaussian noise-prediction training with one additional scale input. We study two sampling processes. ALD-renoise estimates the clean sample and injects fresh marginal noise. ALD-posterior preserves dependence between successive states through an accumulated conditional variance and a Gaussian bridge update. Both samplers reuse the same trained predictor with different scalar inputs. We evaluate ALD on four 2D benchmarks and an imbalanced nine-mode mixture. We also examine training efficiency and the effects of prediction perturbations on clipped Holtsmark data. Additional experiments evaluate MNIST and CelebA64 generation and CIFAR-10LT augmentation. ALD preserves local geometry on the evaluated light-tailed and manifold-structured targets. arXiv Preprint 1 Introduction Diffusion models ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Song and Ermon, 2020 ; Ho et al., 2020 ) have established themselves as the dominant paradigm for high-fidelity generative modeling, with applications spanning image synthesis ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ) and scientific problems ( Pandey et al., 2025 ; Watson et al., 2023 ; Zeni et al., 2025 ) . Their core mechanism is to corrupt data 𝐱 0 ∼ p data \mathbf{x}_{0}\sim p_{\mathrm{data}} via a fixed stochastic process and learn to reverse it: the forward process produces 𝐱 t = m t ​ 𝐱 0 + σ t ​ 𝐧 \mathbf{x}_{t}=m_{t}\mathbf{x}_{0}+\sigma_{t}\mathbf{n} with 𝐧 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝐈 ) \mathbf{n}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}) , and generation proceeds via the estimated reverse kernel p θ ​ ( 𝐱 t − 1 ∣ 𝐱 t ) p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t-1}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}) . The common choice of Gaussian noise is motivated by analytical tractability: it admits closed-form forward kernels, a stable ϵ \epsilon -prediction objective, and a reverse-time SDE representation under suitable regularity conditions via Anderson’s time-reversal formula ( Anderson, 1982 ) . However, for target distributions with polynomial tails, the Gaussian terminal prior and light-tailed perturbation kernels provide exponentially weaker relative coverage of extreme regions than the data law. With finite samples and training budgets, the network therefore struggles to estimate the score accurately in the tail regions due to the scarcity of training samples there. This score estimation difficulty is consequential for a broad and scientifically important class of problems. The Holtsmark distribution describes Coulomb force statistics from random point charges and is a 3 / 2 3/2 -stable distribution ( α = 3 / 2 \alpha=3/2 , with PDF decaying as | x | − 5 / 2 |x|^{-5/2} ) ( Holtsmark, 1919 ; Samorodnitsky and Taqqu, 1994 ; Nolan, 2020 ) ; financial return distributions can exhibit power-law tails, motivating heavy-tailed alternatives to Gaussian models ( Gopikrishnan et al., 1999 ; Nolan, 2020 ; Larralde and Mota Navarro, 2025 ) ; heavy-tailed statistics also arise in fluid dynamics and related transport phenomena, as illustrated by studies of anomalous transport and turbulence spreading ( Solomon et al., 1993 ; Buonocore et al., 2020 ; Milovanov et al., 2025 ) . For such distributions, Gaussian diffusion can suffer from tail blindness : the terminal prior is light-tailed and the training distribution gives sparse effective coverage to rare extremes, so learned scores in tail regions are poorly constrained and may collapse toward bulk-dominated behavior. This bias is not merely a representational limitation: increasing capacity alone does not repair the sparse far-tail coverage induced by Gaussian corruption ( Song and Ermon, 2019 ; Yu and Yu, 2026 ) ; see also Experiment 5.3 . The natural remedy is to replace Gaussian noise with α \alpha -stable Lévy noise ( Applebaum, 2009 ) , whose tail probability decays polynomially as Pr ⁡ ( | z | > x ) ∼ C α ​ x − α \Pr(|z|>x)\sim C_{\alpha}x^{-\alpha} for α ∈ ( 0 , 2 ) \alpha\in(0,2) ; at the boundary α = 2 \alpha=2 the distribution reduces to the Gaussian, whose tails decay exponentially and the polynomial formula no longer applies. This provides a parametric family that can be matched to infinite-variance polynomial-tail targets with tail exponent in ( 0 , 2 ) (0,2) by choosing α \alpha appropriately. However, prior attempts encounter one of two fundamental obstructions. Continuous Lévy–Itô SDE approaches such as LIM ( Yoon et al., 2023 ) require a reverse-time formulation adapted to jump-driven dynamics. Although Lévy processes are semimartingales and admit Itô calculus, the Brownian reverse-SDE formula based on the ordinary score ∇ 𝐱 ​ log ​ p t ​ ( 𝐱 ) \nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\log p_{t}(\mathbf{x}) cannot be applied directly. For isotropic α \alpha -stable noise with α < 2 \alpha<2 , the generator is nonlocal and involves the fractional Laplacian − ( − Δ ) α / 2 -(-\Delta)^{\alpha/2} . LIM derives the corresponding reverse-time formulation using a nonlocal fractional score and learns it through fractional denoising score matching, introducing additional analytical complexity relative to Gaussian diffusion. Discrete Markov chain models such as DLPM ( Shariatian et al., 2025 ) avoid this fractional-score formulation by representing stable noise as a scalar Gaussian scale mixture and deriving approximate reverse updates through conditional Gaussian posterior calculations. Their explicit stable marginal laws rely on convolution closure among independent α \alpha -stable increments with a common stability index. DLPM therefore keeps α \alpha fixed throughout the chain; varying the index would generally take the accumulated noise outside the stable family used in its derivation. Although the noise amplitude can decrease during denoising, this fixed-index construction does not support independently annealing the tail index toward the Gaussian boundary α = 2 \alpha=2 during final refinement. This leaves no tail-index schedule for assigning different tail behavior to exploration and geometry refinement. Recent theoretical and empirical work also identifies a trade-off between improved initialization and the statistical difficulty of reverse estimation under heavy-tailed noising ( Cherkaoui et al., 2026 ) . These paradigms expose complementary modeling constraints: jump-driven formulations require nonlocal reverse operators, while standard fixed-index stable chains do not provide a tail-index schedule. This motivates constructions that keep conditional Gaussian calculations tractable without requiring stable closure across time.
